name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q01 - Respiratory quotient values of substrates and yeast tolerance

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding respiratory parameters and substrates:

List I (Substrate / Condition) List II (Value / Ratio)
A. Carbohydrates (complete oxidation of glucose) I. About 0.9
B. Tripalmitin (fatty acid) II. 1.0
C. Proteins III. About 13 per cent
D. Alcohol concentration lethal to naturally fermenting yeast IV. 0.7

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the respiratory quotient (RQ) of carbohydrates.
When carbohydrates such as glucose are completely oxidised aerobically, the volumes of \(\text{CO}_2\) evolved and \(\text{O}_2\) consumed are equal (\(6\text{CO}_2 / 6\text{O}_2\)), giving an RQ equal to 1.0.

Step 2: Determine the RQ of fats.
When fats like tripalmitin are used in respiration, less oxygen is present in the substrate molecule, requiring more external \(\text{O}_2\) for oxidation. For tripalmitin, \(102\text{CO}_2 / 145\text{O}_2 \approx 0.7\).

Step 3: Determine the RQ of proteins.
When proteins are utilised as respiratory substrates, the ratio of \(\text{CO}_2\) evolved to \(\text{O}_2\) consumed is approximately 0.9.

Step 4: Identify the lethal alcohol concentration for yeast.
During alcoholic fermentation, yeasts poison themselves to death when the concentration of accumulated ethanol reaches about 13 per cent.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Carbohydrates match with 1.0; Tripalmitin matches with 0.7; Proteins match with About 0.9; Alcohol concentration lethal to naturally fermenting yeast matches with About 13 per cent (A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q02 - Enzymes of respiration and their catalytic roles

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding enzymes and the reactions they catalyse in plant respiration:

List I (Enzyme) List II (Catalytic Reaction)
A. Invertase I. Phosphorylation of glucose into glucose-6-phosphate
B. Hexokinase II. Cleavage of sucrose into glucose and fructose
C. Pyruvic acid decarboxylase III. Condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid
D. Citrate synthase IV. Decarboxylation of pyruvate during fermentation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the role of invertase.
Invertase converts sucrose (the end product of photosynthesis) into glucose and fructose, which readily enter the glycolytic pathway.

Step 2: Identify the role of hexokinase.
Hexokinase catalyses the initial phosphorylation of glucose and fructose to form glucose-6-phosphate with the consumption of ATP.

Step 3: Identify the role of pyruvic acid decarboxylase.
In yeast fermentation, pyruvic acid decarboxylase catalyses the conversion of pyruvic acid to acetaldehyde and \(\text{CO}_2\).

Step 4: Identify the role of citrate synthase.
Citrate synthase catalyses the first reaction of the Krebs' cycle: the condensation of the acetyl group from acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid and water to yield citric acid.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Invertase matches with Cleavage of sucrose into glucose and fructose; Hexokinase matches with Phosphorylation of glucose into glucose-6-phosphate; Pyruvic acid decarboxylase matches with Decarboxylation of pyruvate during fermentation; Citrate synthase matches with Condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid (A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q03 - Complexes of the mitochondrial electron transport system

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding the complexes of the electron transport system (ETS):

List I (ETS Complex) List II (Enzyme Complex / Component)
A. Complex I I. Cytochrome c oxidase
B. Complex II II. Cytochrome \(bc_1\) complex
C. Complex III III. NADH dehydrogenase
D. Complex IV IV. Succinate dehydrogenase

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Complex I.
Electrons from matrix NADH produced during the citric acid cycle are oxidised by Complex I, which is NADH dehydrogenase.

Step 2: Identify Complex II.
Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase, through which reducing equivalents from \(\text{FADH}_2\) generated during succinate oxidation enter the electron transport chain.

Step 3: Identify Complex III.
Complex III is the cytochrome \(bc_1\) complex, which transfers electrons from reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) to cytochrome c.

Step 4: Identify Complex IV.
Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, containing cytochromes a and \(a_3\) and two copper centres, which transfers electrons to molecular oxygen.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Complex I matches with NADH dehydrogenase; Complex II matches with Succinate dehydrogenase; Complex III matches with Cytochrome \(bc_1\) complex; Complex IV matches with Cytochrome c oxidase (A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q04 - Intermediates of respiration and their carbon atom numbers

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding respiratory intermediates and the number of carbon atoms they contain:

List I (Intermediate) List II (Carbon Count)
A. Citric acid I. 4 carbons
B. \(\alpha\)-Ketoglutaric acid II. 6 carbons
C. Succinic acid III. 3 carbons
D. Pyruvic acid IV. 5 carbons

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Carbon count of citric acid.
Formed by condensation of a 2-carbon acetyl unit with 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid, citric acid contains 6 carbon atoms.

Step 2: Carbon count of \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid.
After the first oxidative decarboxylation step of the Krebs' cycle, isocitrate loses one molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\) to form \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid, which contains 5 carbon atoms.

Step 3: Carbon count of succinic acid.
After a second oxidative decarboxylation, \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid forms 4-carbon succinyl-CoA, which is subsequently converted into 4-carbon succinic acid.

Step 4: Carbon count of pyruvic acid.
Pyruvic acid is the end product of glycolysis formed from the cleavage and oxidation of hexose sugar, containing 3 carbon atoms.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Citric acid matches with 6 carbons; \(\alpha\)-Ketoglutaric acid matches with 5 carbons; Succinic acid matches with 4 carbons; Pyruvic acid matches with 3 carbons (A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q05 - Cellular compartments and sites of respiratory processes

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding cellular processes and their precise structural sites:

List I (Process / Component) List II (Cellular Location)
A. Glycolysis (EMP pathway) I. Inner mitochondrial membrane
B. Tricarboxylic acid cycle II. Cytoplasm (cytosol)
C. Electron transport system (ETS) III. Peripheral membrane protein complex facing the matrix
D. Catalytic headpiece \(F_1\) of ATP synthase IV. Mitochondrial matrix

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Locate glycolysis.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm (cytosol) of all living cells and does not require oxygen or membrane-bound organelles.

Step 2: Locate the TCA cycle.
The tricarboxylic acid (Krebs') cycle enzymes and reactions take place in the mitochondrial matrix.

Step 3: Locate the ETS.
The electron transport system consists of carrier complexes embedded within the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Step 4: Locate the \(F_1\) headpiece of ATP synthase.
The \(F_1\) headpiece is a peripheral membrane protein complex located on the matrix side of the inner mitochondrial membrane where ATP is synthesised.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Glycolysis matches with Cytoplasm (cytosol); Tricarboxylic acid cycle matches with Mitochondrial matrix; Electron transport system matches with Inner mitochondrial membrane; Catalytic headpiece \(F_1\) of ATP synthase matches with Peripheral membrane protein complex facing the matrix (A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q06 - Key enzymatic steps of glycolysis and their energetic events

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding reactions of glycolysis and their metabolic outcomes:

List I (Reaction in Glycolysis) List II (Energetic / Redox Event)
A. Glucose \(\longrightarrow\) Glucose-6-phosphate I. Reduction of \(\text{NAD}^+\) to \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)
B. Fructose-6-phosphate \(\longrightarrow\) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate II. Substrate-level phosphorylation synthesizing ATP
C. 3-Phosphoglyceraldehyde \(\longrightarrow\) 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate III. First step of ATP utilisation
D. Phosphoenolpyruvate \(\longrightarrow\) Pyruvic acid IV. Second step of ATP utilisation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze reaction A.
The conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate consumes the first molecule of ATP in glycolysis, catalysed by hexokinase.

Step 2: Analyze reaction B.
The conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate consumes the second molecule of ATP, catalysed by phosphofructokinase.

Step 3: Analyze reaction C.
The conversion of 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL) to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA) involves oxidation via removal of two redox-equivalents transferred to \(\text{NAD}^+\), forming \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\).

Step 4: Analyze reaction D.
The conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvic acid involves the transfer of a phosphate group to ADP, resulting in substrate-level synthesis of ATP.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Glucose to Glucose-6-phosphate matches with First step of ATP utilisation; Fructose-6-phosphate to Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate matches with Second step of ATP utilisation; 3-Phosphoglyceraldehyde to 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate matches with Reduction of \(\text{NAD}^+\) to \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\); Phosphoenolpyruvate to Pyruvic acid matches with Substrate-level phosphorylation synthesizing ATP (A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q07 - Substrate entry points into the amphibolic respiratory pathway

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding respiratory substrates and their point of entry into the respiratory pathway:

List I (Substrate) List II (Point of Entry into Pathway)
A. Glycerol I. Converted into acetyl CoA first
B. Fatty acids II. Enters after conversion to PGAL / DHAP
C. Amino acids (proteins) III. Enters as glucose-6-phosphate after initial phosphorylation
D. Glucose IV. Enters as pyruvate, acetyl CoA, or Krebs' cycle intermediates

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Point of entry for glycerol.
Fats are broken down into glycerol and fatty acids. Glycerol enters the respiratory pathway after being converted to 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL) / dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP).

Step 2: Point of entry for fatty acids.
Fatty acids undergo beta-oxidation to form acetyl CoA, entering cellular respiration directly at the acetyl CoA stage.

Step 3: Point of entry for amino acids.
Proteins are hydrolysed into amino acids, which after deamination enter the pathway at different stages depending on their structure: as pyruvate, acetyl CoA, or intermediates within the Krebs' cycle.

Step 4: Point of entry for glucose.
Glucose is the primary substrate; it enters the beginning of glycolysis directly upon phosphorylation to glucose-6-phosphate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Glycerol matches with Enters after conversion to PGAL / DHAP; Fatty acids match with Converted into acetyl CoA first; Amino acids match with Enters as pyruvate, acetyl CoA, or Krebs' cycle intermediates; Glucose matches with Enters as glucose-6-phosphate after initial phosphorylation (A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q08 - Structural components and mobile carriers of the respiratory ETS

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding components of the electron transport system and ATP synthase:

List I (Component) List II (Structural / Functional Feature)
A. Ubiquinone I. Small mobile carrier protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane
B. Cytochrome c II. Contains cytochromes a and \(a_3\), and two copper centres
C. Complex IV III. Integral membrane protein forming a proton-translocating channel
D. \(F_0\) component IV. Inner membrane lipid-soluble carrier receiving electrons from Complex I and Complex II

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural and functional feature of ubiquinone.
Ubiquinone is located within the inner mitochondrial membrane and acts as an electron pool, receiving reducing equivalents from both Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase).

Step 2: Structural and functional feature of cytochrome c.
Cytochrome c is a small peripheral protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane that acts as a mobile carrier transferring electrons between Complex III and Complex IV.

Step 3: Structural and functional feature of Complex IV.
Complex IV refers to cytochrome c oxidase, which possesses cytochromes a and \(a_3\) together with two distinct copper centres (\(\text{Cu}_A\) and \(\text{Cu}_B\)).

Step 4: Structural and functional feature of \(F_0\).
The \(F_0\) component of ATP synthase is an integral membrane protein complex forming a transmembrane channel through which protons diffuse from the intermembrane space into the matrix.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Ubiquinone matches with Inner membrane lipid-soluble carrier receiving electrons from Complex I and Complex II; Cytochrome c matches with Small mobile carrier protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane; Complex IV matches with Contains cytochromes a and \(a_3\), and two copper centres; \(F_0\) component matches with Integral membrane protein forming a proton-translocating channel (A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q09 - Stoichiometry and quantitative parameters of cellular respiration

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding stoichiometric values and parameters described in cellular respiration:

List I (Quantitative Parameter) List II (Numerical Value)
A. Carbon atoms in the acetyl unit entering the TCA cycle I. 38
B. Molecules of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) produced in one turn of the TCA cycle II. 4
C. Number of \(\text{H}^+\) passing through \(F_0\) per ATP synthesized III. 2
D. Net theoretical ATP yield from aerobic respiration of one glucose IV. 3

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine carbon atoms in the acetyl group.
The acetyl unit attached to Coenzyme A contains 2 carbon atoms; it condenses with 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid to yield 6-carbon citric acid.

Step 2: Determine \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) formed per Krebs' cycle turn.
In one turn of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, there are three points where \(\text{NAD}^+\) is reduced to \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) (isocitrate to \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate, \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA, and malate to oxaloacetate).

Step 3: Determine proton translocation per ATP.
For each molecule of ATP produced by the catalytic headpiece \(F_1\), 4 protons (\(4\text{H}^+\)) pass through the \(F_0\) channel from the intermembrane space to the matrix down the electrochemical gradient.

Step 4: Determine net theoretical ATP yield.
The respiratory balance sheet calculates a net theoretical gain of 38 ATP molecules during aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: Carbon atoms in the acetyl unit entering the TCA cycle matches with 2; Molecules of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) produced in one turn of the TCA cycle matches with 3; Number of \(\text{H}^+\) passing through \(F_0\) per ATP synthesized matches with 4; Net theoretical ATP yield from aerobic respiration of one glucose matches with 38 (A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MATCH_Q10 - Distinguishing features of fermentation and aerobic respiration

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding distinct features of respiratory pathways:

List I (Feature / Process) List II (Characteristic / Molecule)
A. End products of fermentation in yeast I. Less than seven per cent
B. End product of anaerobic metabolism in fatigued muscles II. Ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\)
C. Terminal electron and hydrogen acceptor in aerobic respiration III. Molecular oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\))
D. Energy released from glucose during fermentation IV. Lactic acid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify yeast fermentation products.
In yeast under anaerobic conditions, pyruvic acid undergoes decarboxylation and reduction to yield ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\).

Step 2: Identify muscle anaerobic metabolism products.
In exercising animal muscle cells experiencing oxygen deficiency, pyruvic acid is reduced directly to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase.

Step 3: Identify the terminal acceptor in aerobic respiration.
In the electron transport system, molecular oxygen acts as the ultimate electron and hydrogen acceptor, driving the entire chain and forming water.

Step 4: Identify the energy release in fermentation.
In fermentation, there is only partial breakdown of glucose; less than seven per cent of the total chemical energy in glucose is released.

Step 5: Final Conclusion.
The correct pairs are: End products of fermentation in yeast matches with Ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\); End product of anaerobic metabolism in fatigued muscles matches with Lactic acid; Terminal electron and hydrogen acceptor in aerobic respiration matches with Molecular oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)); Energy released from glucose during fermentation matches with Less than seven per cent (A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I).
